title: What Is a Lesson Plan and Why Use One?
brief: Introduce the lesson plan as a practical tool teachers use to design a class session. Draw on the module's description of the blank Lesson Plan Template, which allows teachers to 'specify lesson objectives, skill/content focus areas, lesson sequencing, materials, and procedures' and can be 'modified to suit the needs of their context.' Explain that a completed plan serves as both a preparation guide and a record, referencing the module's note that a filled-in example shows 'the types of information they might include in their own lesson plans.' Do not discuss broader curriculum design or syllabus planning.

title: Background Information and Lesson Objectives
brief: Cover the opening sections of a lesson plan: background information and lesson objectives. Use the Lesson Plan Example from the module, which records course name, institution, lesson length, student ages, gender ratio, occupational backgrounds, motivations, level, and number of students. Then explain lesson objectives using the five numbered 'Students will be able to…' statements from the same example (e.g., orally identifying causes of traffic accidents, listening for gist and detail, using past continuous tense). Also draw on the field 'How does this lesson fit in with the previous and next lessons?' as illustrated in the example, which links the lesson to a prior grammar lesson and a subsequent writing lesson. Do not address materials or procedure in this section.

title: Skills, Content Focus, and Timing
brief: Explain the 'Specific skills/content focus' component using the example's entries: grammar review of the past continuous, listening skills (gist and detail), asking about and reporting events, and theme-based content on road safety. Then address timing, drawing on the module's lesson plan format, which includes a 'Time' column in the procedure table and the detail that the example covers an 80-minute lesson within a 2.5-hour session. Use the ':00' and ':05' time stamps from the example's procedure table to show how timing is recorded stage by stage. Explain what the timing column is for without extending into a full discussion of lesson stages, which is covered in the next section.

title: Procedure and Materials
brief: Explain the procedure and materials columns of a lesson plan, drawing directly on the example's 'Lesson Plan: Time / Procedure / Materials and Rationale' table. Use the warm-up stage described in the module—the teacher displaying four pictures on the whiteboard (woman applying makeup while driving, man on a cell phone, woman texting, man yawning at the wheel)—as a concrete illustration of how a procedure entry is written. Show how the Materials and Rationale column records both what is needed ('printouts of pictures, tape') and why each element is used ('create positive, welcoming atmosphere'; 'create interest; activate prior knowledge'). Also reference the Lesson Plan Template's separate 'Materials' fields and the module's note that each lesson plan lists 'specific materials needed to complete that particular project, with suggestions for variations in case different resources are on hand.'

title: Assessment, Notes, and Pre-Class Preparation
brief: Cover the template fields that sit outside the main procedure table: Assessment, Notes, and Pre-class preparation, all of which appear in the module's Lesson Plan Template. Explain each field's purpose as a place to record what the teacher plans to check or collect, contextual reminders, and tasks to complete before students arrive. Keep descriptions grounded in the template's field labels as presented in the module. Do not invent content not present in the module; focus on what these fields are and what kinds of information belong in them based on their labels and position within the template.

title: Lesson Evaluation: Reflecting After the Class
brief: Explain the Lesson Evaluation section that appears at the end of the module's Lesson Plan Template, using all four questions verbatim as listed: (1) What do you think the students actually learned? How do you know? (2) What parts were most successful/least successful? Why? (3) Did you finish the lesson on time? If not, why? (4) What changes (if any) will you make in your teaching and why (or why not)? Discuss what each question asks the teacher to consider and how completing this section after a lesson connects back to the plan's original objectives and timing. Also reference the module's action-plan prompt that asks teachers to 'reflect on what went well and what you might do differently' and to consider 'alternative approaches or strategies' for the future.
